safety.title: Letting the model override the rules' 'cannot tell' refusals turns deliberate refusals into the model's guess
safety.scenario: Section 4 drops a rules refusal whenever a grounded model quote covers the statement, and it names the 'cannot tell' refusals (unsure() in read_smoking/modify_smoking) as droppable. These refusals are the corpus's X cases: they exist because the phrasing is ambiguous. Checked against the rules: 'not a current smoker', 'quit smoking? no', 'smoker: no (quit 2015)' and 'I no longer smoke a pack a day, down to 5' all give unsure(). An overconfident gpt-5.4-mini returns FormerSmoker with quote = the whole statement and no `unclear` entry. The quote is grounded and covers the statement, so the refusal is dropped and the patient becomes FormerSmoker with cotinine 0. For 'down to 5' the person still smokes, and current vs not is about 8.8 years on the clock. The same happens to 'vapes daily' (vaping problem), 'gestational diabetes' and 'heart disease\nno other conditions' (both 'mentions a medical condition but was not understood' problems): an overconfident model reads them as DIQ010 Yes or MCQ160C Yes. As a result the system can refuse no more often than the small model does, and that model rarely refuses.
safety.fix: Make the rules reader return typed problems: Problem(kind, line, start, end), with kind in {not_understood, ambiguous, contradiction, me_and_someone_else, vaping, unit, lost_condition}. Only kind=not_understood (the 'is about smoking and was not understood' message, and not-understood lines with no _MEDICAL_WORDS) may be replaced by a model reading. ambiguous, contradiction, me_and_someone_else, vaping and the unit statuses stay blocking. The model's reading can appear only as a suggested rephrase ('did you mean: former smoker, quit 2015?'). A lost_condition may be cleared only when the code's own term and polarity check passes on the quote (see the conditions findings), never on the model's word alone.

safety.title: Substring grounding lets a lab take its unit or number from elsewhere in the quote, or from the next line
safety.scenario: Grounding only checks that the number and unit occur somewhere in the quote. (a) 'CRP 2.5, glucose 95 mg/dL': checked, the rules give CRP NEEDS_UNIT. The model returns {LBXCRP, 2.5, unit 'mg/dL', quote: the whole line}. That is grounded, the rules' refusal is dropped, and CRP becomes 2.5 mg/dL = 25 mg/L: 10x too high, and an Elevated witness for the KB. (b) 'HbA1c 6.4 % (was 7.1 % last year)': the rules refuse on the unknown unit (checked); the model's 7.1 is grounded. (c) 'albumin 3.2 g/dL 3.5-5.0': the model picks 3.5 from the reference range, which is grounded. (d) Whitespace collapse lets a quote cross lines. In 'NT-proBNP: not done\nB12 410 pg/mL' the quote grounds SSBNP = 410 pg/mL, a hallucinated high NT-proBNP. (e) Numbers match as plain substrings: 12 matches inside '112', and 1 inside '12'.
safety.fix: Find the quote's span in the original text. Require it to lie inside one source line and one rules statement (no ';' or ', word' boundary crossed). Inside it, the code finds an alias of the claimed lab, then the first number after it with only [:=]/is/of/was/level in between, then the unit text right after that number. In practice this means running _read_lab on the quote from the alias onward. The model's value must equal that number (compared as a bounded token) and its unit must equal normalise_unit of that adjacent text. If the quote holds a second number for the same analyte that is not a recognised 'a-b' reference range, refuse with 'two values for X'.

safety.title: A quote taken from a sentence about someone else passes grounding; the about_someone_else field is never used
safety.scenario: '58 year old\nmy husband smokes': the rules set the second line aside, so they read no smoking and no sex. The model returns CurrentSmoker with quote 'smokes', and Female with quote 'my husband'. Both are substrings, both rules fields are 'nothing', and the patient is built as a current smoker at cotinine level 3 on the female model. '58 year old male\nmy wife is a current smoker' reads OK with no status by the rules (checked), and the model's CurrentSmoker wins. The problem runs the other way too. 'Father: current smoker, diabetes' gives DIQ010=1 from the rules (checked), because _statements splits at ', ' and only the first piece is set aside. The same split gives MCQ160E=1 for 'Family history: diabetes, heart attack' and BPQ020=1 for 'mother: breast cancer, hypertension' (all checked). A model that correctly lists the line under about_someone_else returns nothing for those items, so the 'read X | nothing -> X' row keeps the false Yes.
safety.fix: Map every model quote to its source line and rules statement. Reject it as a problem if that statement was set aside, matches _SOMEONE_ELSE, or overlaps a grounded about_someone_else quote. Apply the same veto to the rules: a rules reading on a line that the model's about_someone_else covers, or on a line where an earlier comma piece was set aside, becomes a 'readers disagree' problem, not X.

safety.title: Answer polarity is not checked, so negation outside the quote flips Yes and No, and the rules' list-negation bug passes as 'rules X | model nothing'
safety.scenario: The rules apply _NEGATION only at the start of each comma piece. Checked: 'negative for diabetes, hypertension' gives BPQ020=1; 'without diabetes, hypertension or stroke' gives BPQ020=1 and MCQ160F=1; 'Denies smoking, diabetes, hypertension' gives DIQ010=1 and BPQ020=1. All of these read ok=True. A small model that lists only positive conditions, or omits the denied ones, hits the 'read X | nothing -> X' row: two false Yes answers, shown as 'rules'. A model that quotes 'hypertension' with answer yes produces 'rules + model', which looks stronger. Negation after the quote: 'borderline diabetes ruled out' is refused by the rules (checked); the model returns DIQ010 borderline with quote 'borderline diabetes', which is grounded, so the refusal is dropped.
safety.fix: Have the code compute polarity for every condition answer, from either reader. Scan from the start of the line, or the last non-comma list boundary, up to the item term for a leading negation (no|not|never|denie[sd]|negative for|without|free of|r/o|ruled out). Then scan the rest of the clause after the term for a trailing one (ruled out|excluded|resolved|negative|\?|: no). A leading negation applies to the whole comma/'or' list after it. If the answer does not match the computed polarity, raise a problem. Add these phrasings to tests/test_patient_text_corpus.py with expected outcomes.

safety.title: The model's lab code settles ambiguities that _resolve deliberately refuses (% vs count, urea vs BUN)
safety.scenario: (a) 'lymphocytes 5' and 'monocytes 1': the rules give NEEDS_UNIT because both % and 10^9/L fit (checked). The model returns LBDLYMNO, or LBXLYPCT, with unit null. The code then calls _resolve([SPECS[code]]), and both choices come back 'ok' (checked). 5 % is lymphopenia and 5 x10^9/L is lymphocytosis, so the model's pick has silently set the clinical meaning. (b) Urea and BUN share LBDSBUSI, and SPECS['LBDSBUSI'] is the BUN row (setdefault, patient_text.py:151-153). For 'my urea came back at 40 mg/dL' the rules read nothing; the model gives LBDSBUSI 40 mg/dL, which converts to 14.28 mmol/L instead of urea's 6.66 (checked). The value is 2.1x too high and inside the NHANES range, so it is accepted.
safety.fix: Do not let the model's code pick the LabSpec. Find the alias in the quote and take specs = the _ALIAS_INDEX entry for it. Require the model's code to be in {s.code for s in specs}, then call _resolve(specs, ...) with all of them, as _read_lab does, so the %/count ambiguity refusal and the urea factor apply. Alternatively, make the enum one value per LabSpec row ('Urea', 'Urea nitrogen (BUN)', 'Lymphocytes %', 'Lymphocytes (count)'), not per NHANES code.

safety.title: Cotinine cannot go through LABS/_resolve, and a censored '<10 ng/mL' becomes level 1
safety.scenario: The design puts LBXCOT into LABS/SPECS and runs it through _resolve. But linage2_model.json gives nhanes_range LBXCOT = (0.0, 2.0), which is the digitised scale, and has no nhanes_central entry (both checked). So the no-unit path raises KeyError in _central. A unit path would mark 250 ng/mL out of range, while 'cotinine 2' (2 ng/mL, a non-smoker) passes as canonical value 2, giving cotinine level 2. Separately, 'cotinine <10 ng/mL', which is how labs commonly report a non-smoker, is not understood by the rules but still reads ok=True (checked). The model returns LBXCOT 10 ng/mL, grounded. _cotinine_level(10) = 1, and 'measured cotinine always wins over words' then overrides 'never smoked': a never-smoker gets level 1. The JSON's own LBXCOT description ('0 Non-smoker, 1 Light/Recent, 2 Heavy/Current') also conflicts with the .metta 0-3 bins, so the scale depends on which description the model is shown.
safety.fix: Keep cotinine out of LABS/SPECS and give it its own path. Accept a value only when 'ng/mL' or 'µg/L' follows the number directly in the quote (then bin with digiCot), or when the literal word 'level' comes with 0-3. Refuse any comparator (<, >, ≤, ≥, 'less than', 'below', 'undetectable', 'negative'), or map '<N' to level 0 only when N <= 10. The enum test should assert that LBXCOT is routed to this path. Show the model only the .metta wording, with an instruction to copy the number exactly as typed.

safety.title: Condition answers can be inferred from medicines or labs, and the 23 items have no NHANES wording, exclusions or time windows
safety.scenario: Nothing requires a condition's quote to name the condition, and the repo has no question text for any of the 23 items (linage2_model.json descriptions has none; checked). So with gpt-5.4-mini: 'on metformin' gives DIQ010 yes; 'BMI 32' gives MCQ160J yes; 'kidney stones' (rules: not understood, ok=True, checked) gives KIQ020 yes, though NHANES 'weak/failing kidneys' excludes stones; 'gestational diabetes' gives DIQ010 yes, though NHANES excludes pregnancy; 'acute bronchitis last winter' gives MCQ160K yes (the item is chronic); 'hospitalized for pneumonia in 2012' gives HUQ070 yes, though the item covers the past 12 months. The rules already read 'hospitalized in 2015' as HUQ070=1 (checked), and a model will agree, so it shows as 'rules + model'.
safety.fix: Give each item a reviewed term list: the rules' _DIAGNOSES pattern plus synonyms. A model answer counts only if its quote contains one of these terms; otherwise it is the problem 'inferred, not stated: write diagnoses: X'. Add per-item exclusions that force a problem: gestational|pregnan for DIQ010; stone|infection for KIQ020; acute for MCQ160K; TIA|mini-stroke for MCQ160F; osteopenia for OSQ060. Allow HUQ070 Yes only with a past-12-months cue, or a date within 12 months of today, and apply that check to the rules' reading too. Put the NHANES 1999-2002 question text into the enum descriptions.

safety.title: other_conditions can clear a rules refusal and turn an ambiguous condition into No
safety.scenario: 'heart disease\nno other conditions' is refused by the rules ('mentions a medical condition but was not understood', checked; the corpus expects False). The model files it as other_conditions [{text: 'heart disease', quote: 'heart disease'}] with no_other_conditions true. The grounded quote covers the statement, so the refusal is dropped. The defaults then answer CHD, angina, heart attack and heart failure all No. The same applies to 'heart trouble', 'kidney problems' and 'lung disease'.
safety.fix: An other_conditions entry whose text or quote matches _MEDICAL_WORDS or any _DIAGNOSES pattern is a problem: 'this may be one of the 23 conditions LinAge2 counts; name it'. Quotes in other_conditions, about_someone_else and unclear never count as covering a rules problem.

safety.title: The lost-condition check uses only the rules' list state, so a list only the model saw answers unread lines No
safety.scenario: '58 year old male\non metformin\nheart trouble': the rules see no list, so 'heart trouble' is only not-understood and the reading is ok (checked). With 'diagnoses: diabetes' in place of 'on metformin' the rules refuse (checked). The model returns DIQ010 yes, quoting 'on metformin'. 'Either reader saw a list' then applies the defaults after the merge, and 'heart trouble' is silently answered No for four cardiac items, with no problem raised.
safety.fix: Run the lost-condition check (patient_text.py:1056-1063) after the merge. Use diagnosed/said_none = the union of both readers, over every not_understood line that a verified (term- and polarity-checked) model condition quote does not cover.

safety.title: Tables and checkbox forms: a whitespace-collapsed quote can swap Yes and No across columns
safety.scenario: 'Smoking   Diabetes   Hypertension\nNo        Yes        No': the rules refuse the first line as smoking 'not understood' (droppable) and do not understand the second (checked). After whitespace collapse, one quote spanning both lines grounds every answer. A small model that misaligns the columns returns DIQ010 No and BPQ020 Yes, and grounding cannot tell. '[x] Hypertension [ ] Diabetes [ ] Stroke' is refused by the rules as a lost line (checked); a model that ignores the box notation answers all three Yes, quoting each name.
safety.fix: For smoking and conditions, require the quote to sit inside one source line and to hold the item term and its answer token next to each other ('diabetes: yes', 'no diabetes', 'never smoked'). A multi-line quote, column layout or bracket checkbox becomes `unclear`, with the problem 'write one condition per line: diabetes: yes'.

safety.title: Every 'rules + model' agreement is trusted, but both readers fail on the same keywords; the rules' wrong readings that agreement would confirm are not in the corpus
safety.scenario: Checked: 'smokes marijuana daily' and 'smokes weed' read as CurrentSmoker level 3, ok=True, with 'marijuana' quietly pushed into not_understood. 'smoking: 0 cigarettes a day' also reads as CurrentSmoker level 3, ok=True. A keyword-driven small model also says CurrentSmoker for cannabis, so the merge shows 'rules + model'. Cannabis produces no cotinine, so the reading adds 8.8 false years. 'lives with a heavy smoker' is also CurrentSmoker by the rules (checked); there the merge is safe only if the model returns nothing.
safety.fix: (a) When a smoking clause has leftover words after _SMOKING_DETAIL (patient_text.py:917-922), block in both readers instead of filing them as not_understood. (b) A non-tobacco lexicon (marijuana|weed|cannabis|pot|joint|hash|meat|fish) in the statement is a problem. (c) A zero count ('0 cigarettes|packs') is refused. (d) 'lives/works with … smoker' is treated as someone else. (e) Add these to the corpus, each with a recorded extraction that AGREES with the wrong rules reading, and assert not-ok, so safety does not depend on the two readers disagreeing.

safety.title: The verification never tests an overconfident model
safety.scenario: Section 7(b) records extractions from 'a capable model following the exact system prompt' (in practice this assistant), which marks ambiguous phrasings unclear. Every corpus X entry then still passes, and the merge's unsafe rows (rules refused | model read -> model; rules X | model nothing -> X) are never exercised by an overconfident reading. In production gpt-5.4-mini returns FormerSmoker for 'not a current smoker' and the tests would not have caught it.
safety.fix: Add an adversarial property test. For every corpus entry expecting X or ok=False, generate every schema-valid, grounded extraction over that statement: each smoking enum value x each intensity with quote = the statement; each item x yes/no/borderline for every condition term present; each lab code whose alias is present x each unit on the line. Assert that the merged result is still not ok. For each ok entry, assert that a grounded but disagreeing extraction gives a problem, never a flipped value. scripts/eval_patient_extraction.py should fail if any X becomes usable with the live model.

safety.title: Values read only by the model are built without anyone confirming them, in the tab and in /patients/from-text
safety.scenario: on_build (patient_tab.py:237-261) re-reads the text and builds in one click; Read is optional, and the textbox is prefilled. 'Ready' is computed, so a model-only CurrentSmoker or condition Yes is built before the person has seen the 'Read by: model' column. /patients/from-text (api.py:2990) returns ok=true plus a patient, while its field description still promises 'Read by fixed rules, no LLM'. And when the in-process cache misses (restart, another worker, eviction), Build calls the model again. Temperature 0 is not determinism, and GPT-5-family reasoning models reject a non-default temperature, so the patient built can differ from the table that was reviewed.
safety.fix: Mark every field read only by the model (smoking status or level, sex, cotinine, any condition answer, GrimAge, weight/height unit) as 'needs confirmation'. Read stores the merged reading under a reading id (a hash of the text, model and prompt version) and lists those fields with their quotes. Build takes that id, refuses if it is missing or stale ('Read again'), never calls the model, and stays disabled until the person ticks that the model readings are right. In the API, model-only fields give ok=false unless the request sets accept_model_readings=true; reading by rules only stays the default, as the API docs promise.

safety.title: Sex can be inferred from indirect cues and override the rules' 'no sex found'
safety.scenario: Sex selects which of LinAge2's two separate models is used. '58 year old, my husband smokes' gives the rules' global 'no sex found' (checked); the model returns Female with quote 'my husband', which is grounded, and the refusal is dropped. 'PSA 1.2' gives Male and 'pregnant in 2010' gives Female, both inferred. For a man with a husband, the whole clock is the wrong model.
safety.fix: Accept sex from the model only when its quote holds an explicit sex token: the rules' _SEX_RES words plus compact forms (58M, 58 y/o F, sex: m/f, M/58). The token must not sit in a someone-else statement. The global 'no sex found' and 'no age found' are otherwise never dropped.

safety.title: Weight, height, GrimAge and visit counts get no number or unit grounding
safety.scenario: Section 3 checks numbers only 'for a lab' and 'for age'. 'weight 90' is refused by the rules ('give the weight's unit', checked). The model returns {90, 'lb'} or {90, 'kg'}; the unit is unchecked, so the reading passes. At 178 cm that gives BMI 12.9 or 28.4, which feeds BMXBMI when BMI is not given. A GrimAge value or a visit count could be hallucinated with any quote.
safety.fix: Apply the same span-local check to every numeric field: number followed by its unit, with the unit literally in the quote. Weight and height without a literal unit stay refused, as the rules refuse them today.

safety.title: is_clock_age, fasting and smoking intensity are model judgements that skip the rules' checks
safety.scenario: 'GrimAge 4' is refused by the rules as a possible clock age (checked). The model sets is_clock_age=false, and AgeAccelGrim +4 goes into the KB's 10-year heart-disease model. For 'glucose 112 mg/dL (drawn 8am)' the rules refuse on the unit text; the model sets fasting=true, the FastingGlucose witness reads Elevated, and the KB credits a glucose cause. Fasting is not in the agreement comparison either. For 'half a pack a day' the rules give level 3; the model says 'moderate', giving level 2. ParsedPatient does not expose the rules' kind, so 'compared only when both are specific' cannot be implemented.
safety.fix: Let the code decide these from the quote, using the rules' own patterns. Treat a GrimAge value as acceleration only when 'accel', 'AgeAccelGrim' or an explicit sign is present; the model's flag may only add a refusal. Set fasting=true only when a _FASTING_ALIASES term precedes the analyte and no non-/not/random/post-prandial token is present, and include fasting in the equality check. Compute the cotinine level from intensity words or packs/cigarettes per day with a code table, and expose the rules' kind. The model's intensity may raise a disagreement but never sets the level.

safety.title: Merging rules' No with the model's borderline across readers hides a disagreement
safety.scenario: The {2,3} -> 3 rule was written for one text that says both 'no diabetes' and 'prediabetes'. Across readers, take 'no diabetes\nHbA1c 6.1 %': the rules give DIQ010=2, and the model adds DIQ010 borderline, quoting 'HbA1c 6.1 %' (a lab-based inference). The merge yields 3 silently, adding one item to fs1Score with no 'readers disagree'.
safety.fix: Allow the cross-reader combination only when the borderline answer's quote contains the rules' prediabetes pattern (pre-?diabet|borderline diabet) and comes from a different statement than the No. Otherwise treat it as a disagreement.

safety.title: 'Covered by the model's quote' cannot be computed from the rules' current output
safety.scenario: Rules problems are plain strings with no span. Some are rewritten: modify_smoking joins two statements with ', ' (so 'smoker; quit 2015' is reported as 'smoker, quit 2015', which is not a substring of the text), and leftover statements are lower-cased and filler-stripped (patient_text.py:922). Short model quotes such as 'diabetes' or 'smoker' can occur several times. An implementation that falls back to fuzzy or substring matching will drop a refusal for one occurrence because of a quote taken from another, for example a negated or someone-else line.
safety.fix: Have _statements and every problem carry (line, start, end) offsets into the original text. A model quote must occur exactly once in the normalised text; otherwise it is ungrounded. A quote covers a problem only when the quote's span contains the problem's span.

kb-consistency.title: The lab enum is keyed by NHANES code, so urea gets the BUN conversion and the reader's %/count and name checks are skipped
kb-consistency.scenario: Two LabSpecs share LBDSBUSI: BUN uses ×0.357 and urea uses ×0.1665 for mg/dL. SPECS uses setdefault, so it keeps only BUN, and patient_vocabulary.vocabulary().labs['LBDSBUSI'] lists only the aliases bun / urea nitrogen / blood urea nitrogen. For 'urea (serum) 40 mg/dL' or 'my urea came back at 40 mg/dL', the rules reader gives not_understood (verified). The model returns LBDSBUSI 40 mg/dL, and code calls _resolve([SPECS['LBDSBUSI']]), giving 14.28 mmol/L with status ok. The correct value is 6.66. For a 58-year-old woman that adds +3.94 LinAge2 years (measured with compute_linage2). When the rules do read 'urea 40 mg/dL' (6.66), the two readers disagree and a clean line is blocked. The same single-spec path drops the rules' NEEDS_UNIT on 'eos 0.2' and 'basophils 0.5': 0.2 is plausible both as % and as 10^9/L, and _resolve([LBXEOPCT]) accepts it as ok. The model also has to tell opaque codes apart: 'MCH 30' coded as LBXMC (MCHC) resolves to 30 g/dL with status ok ('unusual'), not refused.
kb-consistency.fix: Make the enum one value per LABS entry, not per NHANES code. Use a readable key such as 'urea', 'bun', 'lymphocytes', 'mch', 'mchc', with the label, aliases and units carried by code. Map the key back to the alias group (every LabSpec sharing the alias) and call _resolve(group_specs, ...) exactly as _read_lab does. Require one of the chosen spec's aliases to appear, with word boundaries, in the quote; otherwise raise a problem. Never let a model reading replace a rules NEEDS_UNIT / UNKNOWN_UNIT / OUT_OF_RANGE on the same statement. Pin it in tests/test_patient_vocabulary.py: len(vocabulary().labs) == len(LABS) + 1 (LBXCOT), every LabSpec's aliases and units are present, and mapping {'name':'urea','value':40,'unit':'mg/dL'} gives 6.66.

kb-consistency.title: LBXCOT has three conflicting definitions, and the design leaves its code path open (a unitless 'cotinine 3' can become level 3)
kb-consistency.scenario: The KB line the design passes to the model describes LBXCOT as 'digitized ... 0 ... 3 (>=200, a typical daily smoker)'. linage2_model.json describes it as '0 - Non-smoker, 1 - Light/Recent, 2 - Heavy/Current' with nhanes_range [0, 2], and nhanes_central has no LBXCOT key. SPECS has no LBXCOT either; the reader handles cotinine in its own regex branch. For 'cotinine 3', the rules raise 'give cotinine in ng/mL or as level'. The model, primed by the KB text, returns {LBXCOT, 3, unit null}. Row 3 of the merge drops the rules' refusal. If code treats a unitless value as a level, the result is level 3; read as ng/mL it would be level 0. That is 8.8 years for a 58-year-old man (-4.36 vs +4.44). A second chain: for '1 pack a day' the model also emits LBXCOT 1 (the '1' is in the quote, so it is grounded). 'A measured cotinine always wins over words' then makes it level 1 instead of C3, which is -5.9 years. If code instead sends LBXCOT through _resolve/_range/_central, it hits a KeyError (no SPECS entry, no nhanes_central) or refuses level 3 as outside [0, 2].
kb-consistency.fix: Send LBXCOT only to the reader's cotinine branch. ng/mL, µg/L or ug/L go to _cotinine_level. A unitless value is accepted only when the quote contains 'level' and the value is in {0,1,2,3}; anything else is a problem. Require 'cotinine' in the quote. Describe the code to the model as 'a serum cotinine TEST RESULT in ng/mL, only when a cotinine value is written', not with the KB's digitized text. Never drop the rules' cotinine refusal. Fix linage2_model.json: the LBXCOT description to 0-3, and nhanes_range to [0, 3] or remove it. Add drift checks that cotinine_levels keys == {'0','1','2','3'} and that the vocabulary's cotinine units equal the reader's (today vocabulary says ['ng/mL'], the reader also takes µg/L and ug/L).

kb-consistency.title: The intensity enum (light|moderate|heavy|unknown) does not map onto the reader's or the KB's cotinine levels
kb-consistency.scenario: The reader and the KB comment ('3 = a typical daily smoker') give level 3 to every daily or unspecified current smoker. Only the words light, occasional, social, some days or weekends give 1, and only 'moderate' gives 2. The corpus pins 'smokes 10 cigarettes a day' as C3. A model following clinical convention labels it 'moderate', which means level 2 (-2.9 y). The other option, treating the rules' level as 'specific', blocks a C3 line the corpus requires to be ok. 'half a pack a day' has the same problem. The design also says 'words -> level from intensity' without gating on status. 'former heavy smoker' (corpus F, level 0) comes back FormerSmoker/heavy and, if mapped naively, becomes level 3: +8.8 y, and it contradicts linage2_core §5 that cotinine measures CURRENT exposure. Nothing defines a level for intensity 'unknown'.
kb-consistency.fix: Replace the enum with the reader's kinds: occasional_or_light | moderate | daily_or_unspecified. Map them in one code function: Never/Former → 0. Current → 1 only if a light/occasional/social/some-days/weekend word is in the quote, 2 only if 'moderate' is in the quote, otherwise 3. A cigarettes-per-day count never lowers the level. Pin it with a test that runs every C1/C2/C3/F/N entry of tests/test_patient_text_corpus.py SMOKING through this mapping with each intensity value, and asserts the level equals the reader's _SMOKING level for that kind.

kb-consistency.title: Vaping, nicotine replacement and the rules' smoking refusals can be overridden, so the KB's cessation gate fires for a non-smoker
kb-consistency.scenario: The status enum offers only Never/Former/Current/unclear/not_stated. linage2_core §6 says LBXCOT also responds to second-hand exposure and nicotine replacement, and pln_linage2 credits cotinine years to SmokingCessation only for (PatientSmoking P CurrentSmoker). For 'vapes daily' (corpus X), the rules raise 'vaping raises cotinine but is not smoking to the knowledge base'. The model returns CurrentSmoker, row 3 ('nothing/refused | read Y → Y; the rules' refusal is dropped') drops the refusal, and the patient gets level 3 (+4.4 y) plus a quit-smoking counterfactual that credits years quitting cigarettes would not remove. 'on nicotine patches' (rules: 'about smoking and was not understood') goes the same way. So do the 'cannot tell' X cases, for example 'smoked for 20 years' read as FormerSmoker (level 0).
kb-consistency.fix: Add smoking.other_nicotine: none|vaping|nrt|snus|secondhand. Code refuses, as the rules do, when the smoking quote matches patient_text._VAPING or nicotin* and not smok|cig|tobacco. For smoking, row 3 must not apply: a status is used only when both readers agree, or when the rules read nothing and raised no problem. A rules smoking problem ('cannot tell...', vaping, 'not understood') is never dropped. Keep every SMOKING 'X' row of the corpus as an X in the merged-reader test.

kb-consistency.title: Self-rated health, its trend and healthcare visits are judged by the model, unchecked, and they are worth several LinAge2 years
kb-consistency.scenario: No .metta file declares answer codes for HUQ010, HUQ020 or HUQ050. The KB only has prose in the fs2Score/fs3Score comments, so these enums cannot come from the KB. Their real sources are patient_text._HEALTH/_TREND/_visits_category and linage2_model._ANSWER_CODES. §3 grounds only lab numbers and age, so any quote substring passes. 'health is so-so' or 'not great' mapped to fair gives +1.76 y (male) / +2.15 y (female). With 'worse than last year' that becomes +3.5 / +4.3, and 'poor' is +3.5 / +4.3 on its own. If visits is an enum of NHANES categories, the model does the binning: 'I see my doctor every month' becomes category 4, +2.5 y for a woman; category 5 is +3.1 y. All measured with compute_linage2 at age 58.
kb-consistency.fix: HUQ010 and HUQ020: the chosen scale word (excellent / very good / good / fair / poor; better / worse / about the same) must appear in the quote, not negated; otherwise raise a problem. Visits: the schema returns an integer count, the count (or once/twice/none) must be in the quote, and code bins it with _visits_category. Pin it in the drift test: set(_HEALTH.values()) ⊆ _ANSWER_CODES['HUQ010'], set(_TREND.values()) ⊆ _ANSWER_CODES['HUQ020'], the range of _visits_category ⊆ _ANSWER_CODES['HUQ050'], and patient_vocabulary.HEALTH_ITEMS == FS2_ITEMS + FS3_ITEMS.

kb-consistency.title: The fasting flag is not grounded, yet it creates the KB's FastingGlucose witness
kb-consistency.scenario: kb_markers emits FastingGlucose only when glucose.fasting is true. linage2_core §5 explains why: (MeasuresBiomarker SerumGlucose FastingGlucose), and 'a non-fasting reading ... overstates insulin resistance'. The schema puts a fasting boolean on every lab, but §3 grounds only the number and unit. Take 'Labs this morning:' and 'glucose 112 mg/dL'. The rules read 6.2 mmol/L, not fasting, and add a note. The model sets fasting=true with the quote 'glucose 112 mg/dL'. The values agree, so the row reads 'rules + model', and the table never says whose fasting flag wins. If the model's flag wins: z = (112-95)/12 = 1.42 > 1.0, so Elevated, and the KB credits the glucose contribution to the metabolic axis and AMPK activators.
kb-consistency.fix: Add a nullable fasting_quote. fasting=true only if fasting_quote is grounded and matches fast|fbg|fpg, and only for LBDSGLSI; ignore the flag on every other code. When the readers disagree on fasting, use false and add the reader's existing note ('write fasting glucose ... if it was'). Add a unit test with recorded JSON: glucose quote without 'fasting' plus fasting=true gives no FastingGlucose marker.

kb-consistency.title: A substring-only check lets the model infer sex, and sex selects the LinAge2 model
kb-consistency.scenario: §3 checks only that the sex quote is a substring of the text. Take '58 year old, my wife and I...': the rules set the statement aside and raise 'no sex found'. The model returns Male with quote 'my wife', which is grounded, and row 3 makes it the sex. Words like 'PSA 1.2' or 'hysterectomy' behave the same way. compute_linage2 then uses the other sex-specific model; the tab's '58-year-old smoker' example scores 13.28 as Male vs 11.43 as Female. build_patient also records the guessed sex in the KB.
kb-consistency.fix: Accept a model sex only when the quote contains an explicit sex token: the reader's _SEX_RES words, 'sex: m/f', or an age+M/F form such as '58M' / '58 F' (that last form is where the model adds value). Anything else is a problem ('state male or female'). Add the 'my wife' and 'PSA' cases to the merged-reader tests as refusals.

kb-consistency.title: Condition answers are not checked against _ANSWER_CODES, and the design overstates what fs1Score counts
kb-consistency.scenario: answer: yes|no|borderline is offered for all 23 items, but linage2_model._ANSWER_CODES allows 3 only for DIQ010. For 'borderline hypertension', the rules refuse it (verified, 'not understood' problem). The model returns BPQ020 borderline, the refusal is dropped, and BPQ020=3. The read table says Ready, then compute_linage2 raises linage2_invalid_questionnaire at Build: HTTP 422 from /patients/from-text, 'Not built' in the tab. Separately, 'heart disease\nno other conditions' (corpus: refused) is mapped by the model to MCQ160C, and its 'not understood' problem is dropped. The design's '23 items fs1Score counts' is also wrong: linage2_model.FS1_ITEMS and the JSON's derived.fs1Score.from have 22, since MCQ160B is read but not counted. Each item adds 1/22 × ~0.7-0.95 months, essentially 0 y, which the read table never says.
kb-consistency.fix: Map yes→1, no→2, borderline→3 and validate against _ANSWER_CODES[item] when the text is read: borderline on anything but DIQ010 is a problem. A rules refusal raised because _MEDICAL_WORDS matched but no item could be placed ('heart disease', 'heart problems') stays. Add drift checks: set(linage2_model.FS1_ITEMS) | {'MCQ160B'} == set(vocabulary().conditions) == set(model['derived']['fs1Score']['from']) | {'MCQ160B'}. Correct the design text to '23 read, 22 counted (MCQ160B not counted)'.

kb-consistency.title: drift() passes today even though the KB, the JSON and the reader disagree on units, and the model is told the wrong unit
kb-consistency.scenario: URXUCRSI: linage2_core.metta and linage2_model.json say 'mmol/L', but the reader and NHANES use µmol/L (nhanes_range 177-68422). LBXCRP: the JSON says 'mg/L', while the KB and the reader say mg/dL. LBXCOT: the JSON says 0-2. drift() returns []. The design passes the KB descriptions to the model. For 'urine creatinine 9.8', the rules read it correctly (unit assumed mmol/L, 9800 µmol/L), but the model may fill in 'mmol/L' from the description; that unit is not in the quote, and per §3 this blocks a correct reading. The tab's own EXAMPLES fail the same way: 'blood pressure 142/88' and 'pulse 78' have descriptions saying mmHg and beats/min, so a model that fills in the unit blocks them.
kb-consistency.fix: Correct the URXUCRSI structured comment in linage2_core.metta to µmol/L, and correct the JSON descriptions for URXUCRSI, LBXCRP and LBXCOT. Add to drift(): the parenthesised unit of each KB description, after normalise_unit, is in SPECS[code].units with scale (1,0), and the same for model.description(code). When a model unit is not in the quote, drop it and resolve the value as unitless; _resolve already refuses an ambiguous unitless value. Do this instead of raising a blocking problem.

kb-consistency.title: GrimAge: the model's is_clock_age replaces the rules' test, the sign is not grounded, and the KB's residual-versus-difference distinction is lost
kb-consistency.scenario: For 'grimage 4.5', the rules refuse (no 'accel', no sign, so possibly a clock age). The model returns is_clock_age=false, the refusal is dropped, and AgeAccelGrim is +4.5. For 'GrimAge 3 years younger' (rules: not understood), +3 and -3 both pass a number-in-quote check. At ±5 y the difference is z ±1.19, Elevated vs Low, in the CHD model's HR^years. The KB defines AgeAccelGrim as the residual ((ResidualOf AgeAccelGrim GrimAge); nhanes_baseline.metta says the definition is 'never assumed by the reader'). Yet the reader's refusal message asks for 'clock age minus your age', which is the difference.
kb-consistency.fix: Schema: grimage {quote, magnitude, direction: older|younger|signed|unstated, wording: acceleration|clock_age|unstated}. Code applies the rules' own test to the quote: one of 'accel', an explicit sign, or 'ageaccelgrim' must be present. It takes the sign from '-' or 'younger'/'older' in the quote and refuses when the direction is unstated. Change the refusal message to ask for the acceleration as the report gives it, not to compute clock age minus age.

kb-consistency.title: The design's lab-enum source contradicts the KB and the committed vocabulary, and nothing says which wins when LDL and the three lipids are both typed
kb-consistency.scenario: §1 builds the enum from ModelInput lines that are direct inputs and says LABS/SPECS must cover exactly these. Those lines hold 54 codes. They exclude LBDTCSI, LBDHDLSI and LBDSTRSI, which the KB says are 'NOT model inputs ... consumed into the calculated LDL', and LDLV is a §4b derived line. Built that way, 'total cholesterol 228 mg/dL, HDL 41, triglycerides 190' has no enum value, and drift() would fail against SPECS. The committed core/patient_vocabulary.py actually uses SPECS ∪ {LBXCOT}, 58 codes, so the design text is wrong. 'A test asserts the enums equal what the .metta files declare' holds only for the smoking statuses and the 59 feature codes. Separately, with all three lipids plus a typed lab LDL (usually Friedewald, TG/2.2), compute_linage2 uses the typed LDL: 3.75 mmol/L instead of the KB's TC - HDL - TG/5 = 4.41 for that panel.
kb-consistency.fix: Rewrite §1 to name the real sources: labs = model.lab_inputs ∪ {LDLV} (= SPECS ∪ LBXCOT); conditions = questionnaire_items - HEALTH_ITEMS from the JSON; only the statuses and features come from .metta. When all three lipids are present, derive LDLV as the KB defines it, ignore the typed LDL for the model, and note this in the read table.

kb-consistency.title: OpenAI strict schema: within the size limits, but nullable enums and key order need care
kb-consistency.scenario: Sizes are fine: about 110 enum values (limit 1000), under 100 properties (limit 5000), nesting depth 3 (limit 10). However: (1) 'sex {Male|Female|null}' and the nullable health and trend enums written as type:['string','null'] with enum ['Male','Female'] do not admit null, because null fails an enum that does not list it. The constrained decoder then has to pick Male or Female when the text says nothing. (2) Structured Outputs emits keys in schema order. The design puts quote last ({code, value, unit, fasting, quote}), so the model commits to code and value before it copies the text, and the quote becomes a justification written afterwards. (3) Bare enum values like 'LBXMC' and 'LBXMCHSI' give the decoder nothing to tell them apart, and JSON Schema has no per-value descriptions.
kb-consistency.fix: Use enum lists that contain null (or anyOf [{enum}, {type:'null'}]) for every nullable enum, and keep top-level objects non-null with nullable leaves. Put quote first in every object, and why_unclear before status. Use readable enum keys, or anyOf of {const, description}, mapped to codes in Python. Add a test that validates a recorded all-null extraction against the generated schema with jsonschema.

kb-consistency.title: An unsupported model or parameter silently leaves the tab on rules only
kb-consistency.scenario: PLN_EXTRACT_MODEL defaults to config.DEFAULT_MODEL, which is os.getenv('PLN_MODEL'). AVAILABLE_MODELS includes gpt-4-turbo, which does not support response_format json_schema. A user who set PLN_MODEL=gpt-4-turbo for chat gets a 400 on every extraction. llm_translator._classify_api_error maps it to 'upstream_error', and §5 falls back to 'read by rules only: <reason>' forever. temperature=0 on a GPT-5-family reasoning configuration can fail the same way. Neither case is checked: finish_reason=='length' (truncated JSON) and message.refusal. requirements.txt pins openai>=1.0, but json_schema and .parse need >=1.40.
kb-consistency.fix: Give PLN_EXTRACT_MODEL its own default, checked at startup against an allowlist of models that support structured outputs. Classify a 400 whose param is response_format or temperature as 'model_unsupported' and show it as a configuration error, not a fallback. Check finish_reason and refusal explicitly. Pin openai>=1.40. Make scripts/eval_patient_extraction.py fail if any text came back rules-only.

kb-consistency.title: A single height value cannot hold 5'10", so BMI comes out wrong or a correct reading is blocked
kb-consistency.scenario: height {value, unit, quote}. The rules read 'height 5\'10"' as 177.8 cm. The model can return 70 in, which is not in the quote, so it is ungrounded and blocks a line the rules read. It can return 5.83 ft, also ungrounded. Or it can return 5 ft, which is grounded and gives 152 cm. For a phrasing the rules miss ('I'm 5 foot 10'), that last one is used. With weight 80 kg it gives BMI 34.6 instead of 25.3, and BMXBMI is a LinAge2 input.
kb-consistency.fix: Height becomes {quote, feet, inches, cm, m}, all nullable, and code converts it with the reader's own arithmetic. Or the model returns only the quoted height text and code parses it with the reader's height regexes. Add a recorded-JSON test for 5'10" and '5 foot 10'.

ux-failure.title: The NHANES-code enum forces a guess where the rules ask (percent vs count) and converts urea as if it were BUN
ux-failure.scenario: 'lymphocytes 5' with no unit: the rules return needs a unit, because it could be 5 % or 5x10^9/L. The schema's lab enum makes the model choose LBXLYPCT or LBDLYMNO. Code then resolves against that one spec (`_resolve([SPECS[code]], 5, '')` returns ok; I checked this), and §4 row 3 drops the rules' refusal. The result is a coin-flip between a normal differential and severe lymphocytosis. Monocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils behave the same way. Separately, SPECS['LBDSBUSI'] is the BUN spec (built with setdefault). So 'my urea was 30 mg/dL', which the rules leave unread, becomes 30 x 0.357 = 10.7 mmol/L and is accepted as ok. The correct value with the urea factor of 0.1665 is 5.0. And 'urea 30 mg/dL', which the rules read correctly as 4.995, turns into a permanent 'the two readers disagree' that no rewording can clear.
ux-failure.fix: Make the model's lab enum the analyte name, one entry per distinct alias group in `_ALIAS_INDEX` ('lymphocytes', 'urea', 'urea nitrogen (BUN)', …), generated in patient_vocabulary. Do not use the NHANES code. Code then resolves with that group's whole spec list, exactly as `_read_lab` does (`_resolve(group_specs, …)`). Percent-vs-count then stays needs a unit, and urea keeps its own factor. Extend drift(): any alias group with more than one spec, and any code shared by specs with different factors, must be its own enum entry.

ux-failure.title: Numbers and units come from the model; a substring check lets wrong values through and blocks right ones
ux-failure.scenario: (a) Wrong value accepted: for 'my platelet count was 245', which the rules leave unread, the model returns 45. '45' is a substring of the quote, so it counts as grounded, and 45x10^9/L is used. (b) Typed unit dropped: the model returns unit null for 'albumin 4.2 g/L'. The 'unit (if any)' check passes, and `_resolve` takes the no-unit path, giving 42 g/L with the unit assumed (I checked this). Row 3 then drops the rules' out-of-range refusal ('did you mean g/dL?'), which is the exact case the module docstring leads with. (c) False ungrounding: for 'creatinine .9 mg/dL', which the rules read, the model returns 0.9. '0.9' is not in '.9', so the item is ungrounded and blocking. The same happens with '1,250' vs 1250 and with 112.0 formatted as '112.0'.
ux-failure.fix: Remove value and unit from the schema. The model returns {name, quote}, and code parses the number and the unit text out of the quote with the rules' own `_NUM` and trailing-unit capture (exactly one number after the name, otherwise unclear), then calls `_resolve`. Do the same for age (`_AGE_RES` on the quote), weight and height (the rules' regexes) and GrimAge. Grounding then means 'the rules' parse of the quote succeeded', and no number from the model ever reaches LinAge2.

ux-failure.title: Row 3 lets a model guess override the rules' deliberate 'cannot tell' refusals, and the recorded-corpus check cannot detect it
ux-failure.scenario: 'smoked for 20 years', 'not a current smoker', 'heavy smoker? not sure' and 'vapes daily' are all corpus X cases: the rules refuse them, and levels 0 and 3 are about 8.8 years apart. gpt-5.4-mini can plausibly return FormerSmoker or NeverSmoker with the whole line as the quote. The quote is grounded, the rules' refusal on that statement is dropped, and the patient is built. Verification (b) runs on extractions written by 'a capable model following the prompt', not by gpt-5.4-mini. So it shows the merge works with a careful reader and says nothing about this failure.
ux-failure.fix: (1) Never drop a rules problem that is a judgement: cannot tell, contradiction, needs a unit, unknown unit, out of range, duplicate. The model may only fill statements the rules listed as not understood. (2) Never use a smoking status from the model alone. Show it as a blocking suggestion: "read as 'former smoker' — [Use this wording]". The button writes that phrase into the textbox and the rules read it. (3) Test the merge against a hostile model, offline: for every corpus X text, merge every schema-valid smoking answer (each status plus unclear/not_stated, times each intensity, about 20 per case) and assert the outcome stays X. For every needs-a-unit case, merge every code in its alias group with unit null.

ux-failure.title: Build can use a reading the person never saw, because the cache semantics are underspecified
ux-failure.scenario: Read times out (the config's 60 s timeout with 1 retry) and the table says 'rules only'. on_build then calls the reader again. The design does not say failures are cached, so Build calls the model, gets an answer, and builds from a merged reading that was never shown. The reverse also happens: Read showed 'rules + model, Ready', then a restart, hot reload or LRU eviction makes Build miss the cache, the call fails, and Build falls back to rules only and says 'Not built' with problems the table never showed. The cache key is the text hash only, so changing PLN_EXTRACT_MODEL or the prompt in a running dev server keeps serving old extractions. The .metta download header ('send the same text again to rebuild it') stops being true once a model is in the loop.
ux-failure.fix: Have Read put the merged ParsedPatient together with its source text into a gr.State; the tab already threads gr.State. Build takes that State, refuses with 'the text changed since Read — press Read' if the textbox differs, and never calls the model. Write the canonical 'read as' text into the download header so the patient can be rebuilt offline with the rules alone. Keep a cache only to save cost: key it on sha256(model | prompt hash | schema hash | text), store failures too, and cap it with an LRU of about 128.

ux-failure.title: The `unclear` list and the intensity comparison will block clear text, including the shipped example and corpus rows
ux-failure.scenario: Given an `unclear` list, a mini model will flag 'WBC 8.2', 'BMI 29.4' and 'pulse 78' (all unitless lines in EXAMPLES['58-year-old smoker']) as 'no unit given', or 'takes lisinopril' and 'vegetarian' with topic other. The row 'any | unclear → problem' blocks each one. The default example is then never Ready, and corpus rows such as 'diagnoses: hypertension\ntakes lisinopril' (expected ok=True) fail. On intensity: 'smokes 10 cigarettes a day' is C3 in the corpus, but 'moderate' is a natural model answer for 10 a day. That gives level 2 against the rules' 3, so 'the two readers disagree' and the case flips to X. The design also does not say whether the rules' default level 3 for 'current smoker' counts as 'specific'.
ux-failure.fix: Let `unclear` block only for topic smoking, or for a condition the model names among the 23. Lab and other unclear items become notes, since units are judged by `_resolve`, not by the model. Shrink the intensity enum to {occasional, not_occasional_or_unstated}. Occasional maps to level 1, and only when the quote contains an occasional word. Level 2 comes only from the rules' literal 'moderate smoker'. Treat it as a disagreement only when one side says occasional and the other gives an explicit daily or pack count; otherwise use the rules' level.

ux-failure.title: Ungrounded items and model silence block the build, so the model's own sloppiness becomes something the person cannot fix
ux-failure.scenario: The model quotes 'HbA1c 6.4%' for 'HbA1c 6.4 %', 'Current smoker.' with an added period, or '58-year-old male' for '58 year old male'. Casefolding and whitespace collapse do not make these substrings of the text. Each produces "could not find '…' in your text" on a line the rules read perfectly, and nothing the person types changes what the model quotes. For smoking, the row 'rules read X / model nothing → problem' turns one bad quote into a blocked build of the default example. In the other direction there is a hole: an empty quote is a substring of every text, so a condition with quote '' counts as grounded.
ux-failure.fix: Discard an ungrounded item, list it in a collapsed debug <details>, and treat it as 'the model said nothing'. 'The model said nothing' never blocks, for any field including smoking: rules X with model silent gives X, plus a note 'the model did not confirm this'. Only an actual contradiction (X vs Y) blocks. Compare quotes after removing all whitespace and punctuation, match on token boundaries, and require at least 3 non-space characters, so that '' or 'm' never grounds anything.

ux-failure.title: Conditions can be inferred from labs or medication lines and still pass grounding
ux-failure.scenario: EXAMPLES['58-year-old smoker'] contains 'HbA1c 6.4 %', 'BMI 29.4' and 'diagnoses: hypertension'. Asked to fill the 23 items, the model may add DIQ010 borderline (quote 'HbA1c 6.4 %') or MCQ160J (quote 'BMI 29.4'). Both quotes are verbatim, so both are grounded. The rules gave those items only the default No, and §4 applies defaults after the explicit answers are merged. So the model's borderline wins with no disagreement, and fs1Score changes on the shipped demo text. 'on metformin' → diabetes Yes works the same way. 'Nothing the text does not say' does not hold.
ux-failure.fix: Use a condition item only if its quote contains a word from that item's own pattern (the item's `_DIAGNOSES` regex, or a per-item synonym list generated in patient_vocabulary), and the quote is not a lab or vital line (`_read_lab` or the BP regex can read it). Otherwise show a note: "the model inferred prediabetes from 'HbA1c 6.4 %' — write 'prediabetes' if a doctor told you so".

ux-failure.title: The rules' problems are free-text strings, so 'drop the rules' refusal for a statement the model's quotes cover' cannot be implemented
ux-failure.scenario: `ParsedPatient.problems` is list[str], and `not_understood` holds filler-stripped leftovers. '58 year old male with a history of heart trouble' gives not_understood ['with history of heart trouble'] (I checked this). That string is not a substring of any verbatim quote ('with a history of heart trouble'). 'hypertension on lisinopril' appears only inside a problem sentence. So coverage either never matches, which over-refuses because the model's reading and the rules' problem both stay, or it ends up done by fuzzy matching, which under-refuses.
ux-failure.fix: In `read_patient_text`, record each statement's (line, start, end) span from `_statements`. Attach it to every Reading, every problem and every not-understood entry: problems become a small dataclass {span, kind, message}, and `all_problems()` still returns the strings so the tests and the API stay unchanged. Locate each model quote in the original text to a span. Coverage means span overlap, and only kind == not_understood can be dropped.

ux-failure.title: The model would be called at UI construction and on every example click, with the shared 60 s × 2 timeout
ux-failure.scenario: build_tab renders `gr.Markdown(on_read(EXAMPLES['58-year-old smoker']))` at layout time, and each example button calls on_read. If on_read calls the model, app startup and every UI build in tests make a network call. In this container api.openai.com is blocked, so startup can hang for up to OPENAI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=60 with OPENAI_MAX_RETRIES=1. Every example click is a paid call on text the rules already read cleanly (test_the_tab_examples_still_read_cleanly). Gradio's default concurrency limit of 1 per event also queues every other viewer behind one slow Read.
ux-failure.fix: Use `on_read(text, use_model=False)` for the initial render and the example buttons; call the model only from the Read button. Give the extractor its own client with PLN_EXTRACT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS≈20 and max_retries=0, so the rules-only fallback appears within 20 s. Use `read_btn.click(..., concurrency_limit=4)`. Put the static instructions and vocabulary first and the user's text last, so OpenAI's automatic prefix caching (≥1024 tokens) cuts latency and cost. Have the eval script report p50/p95 latency and token counts.

ux-failure.title: Tests and the battery make live calls whenever a developer's .env holds a key
ux-failure.scenario: config.py calls load_dotenv(). tests/test_patient_text_corpus.py (239 cases), tests/test_patient_tab.py and scripts/linage2_battery.py all call read_patient_text, on_read or on_build. With the model inside those paths, a developer's test run makes about 300 paid calls, results change from run to run, and the battery PDF churns (it already masks temp-file suffixes precisely to avoid churn).
ux-failure.fix: Keep `read_patient_text` rules-only and pure, so the corpus keeps pinning the rules unchanged. Add `read_patient(text, extractor)` and use it only from the Read button and from the API with reader='model'. Tests pass a RecordedExtractor backed by JSON fixtures. Add an autouse conftest fixture that makes the OpenAI extractor raise if it is invoked, unless PLN_LIVE_EXTRACT=1. The battery passes use_model=False and prints 'reader: rules' in the PDF.

ux-failure.title: A 'Read by' column breaks pinned strings and misses the field that matters most
ux-failure.scenario: The battery's t_albumin_ok asserts the full row '| Albumin | `albumin 4.1 g/dL` | 41 g/L | ✓ | 45 g/L |', so any new column fails it. Offline, every row would say 'rules', which is noise. Smoking, age, sex and the conditions are not table rows. A model-only smoking status, the largest lever in the patient, would have no 'read by' at all.
ux-failure.fix: Add no column. Rules-only rows stay byte-identical. A row that came from the model gets '· model' appended in the Check cell, with its quote in 'You typed'. The who line names the source for smoking, age and sex, e.g. 'Smoking FormerSmoker — model, from "quit when my son was born"'. Add one header line: 'Read by rules + gpt-5.4-mini', or 'Read by rules only — no OPENAI_API_KEY', or '— model timed out after 20 s'.

ux-failure.title: A disagreement message gives the person no way to resolve it
ux-failure.scenario: For 'urea 30 mg/dL' (see the enum finding) or a smoking clause, the problem 'the two readers disagree' does not tell the person which reading is right. Rewording a line that is already in canonical form can never converge, so the person cannot build at all.
ux-failure.fix: Each disagreement names both readings with their values, plus the exact phrase each reader accepts ("write 'former smoker' or 'current smoker'"). A [Use this wording] button replaces the clause in the textbox and reads again. Add a rule: a statement the rules read as ok, whose text already equals its canonical form (alias + number + unit, or one of the canonical smoking phrases), is authoritative, and a model disagreement there is only a note. Then typing the canonical phrase always resolves a disagreement.

ux-failure.title: The /patients/from-text contract changes silently, and the endpoint exposes cost
ux-failure.scenario: PatientTextIn.text and the endpoint docstring both say 'Read by fixed rules, no LLM'. API keys and rate limiting are off by default, and config.py mentions keeping an ngrok tunnel to the UI port working. So anyone who can reach it can POST 20,000-character texts, each becoming a paid strict-schema call. The sync handler holds a threadpool worker for up to about 2 minutes on a timeout. test_the_api_reads_text_into_the_same_patient asserts that the tab and the API build the same patient.
ux-failure.fix: Add `reader: Literal['rules','model'] = 'rules'` to PatientTextIn; extra='forbid' keeps old request bodies valid. The response adds `reader_used`, `model_error` (an ERROR_CODES value) and a per-reading `source`. reader='model' requires a configured key and text of at most about 4,000 characters (otherwise 413). Bump PLN_API_VERSION to 2.1.0 and update API.md. The tab says 'Read sends your text to OpenAI (<model>)' next to the button.

ux-failure.title: Some failure modes would quietly look like 'rules only' and hide a broken setup
ux-failure.scenario: Structured outputs report a refusal in `message.refusal` with `content` None. Copying llm_translator's `content or ""` → json.loads pattern would label that 'bad_json'. finish_reason 'length' (a long text, or reasoning tokens using up max_completion_tokens) truncates the JSON. A strict-schema 400 makes every single call fail, and the demo just says 'rules only' indefinitely. Typical causes are a nullable enum without null in its value list, a property missing from `required`, or `additionalProperties` not set to false.

Show the error code in the header line. scripts/eval_patient_extraction.py makes one schema-acceptance call first and exits non-zero on a 400. ux-failure.title: Simplest design that keeps the safety properties: the model fills gaps as canonical lines, the rules read everything, Build reads the stored result
ux-failure.scenario: Every finding above comes from the five-row merge and its special cases, each of which assumes the model behaves well: dropped refusals, intensity comparison, defaults applied after the merge, coverage by quote, unclear treated as blocking. Consistency with the .metta files then depends on two parallel conversion paths agreeing.
ux-failure.fix: (1) The model returns only enums plus quotes, no numbers: lab name-group, smoking status + occasional, condition item + yes/no/borderline, sex, plus quotes for age/weight/height/GrimAge/health answers. (2) Code turns each grounded item into a line in the rules' own grammar, copying the number and unit text from the quote: 'albumin 4.1 g/dL', 'former smoker', 'diagnoses: hypertension', 'no diabetes', '58 year old', 'female'. A round-trip test over the whole vocabulary asserts rules(render(item)) == item; together with the existing drift() test, this is what guarantees consistency with patient_profile.metta and linage2_core.metta. (3) Using the statement spans, substitute canonical lines only into statements the rules did not understand. Judgement refusals and any smoking status from the model alone become [Use this wording] suggestions, never silent substitutions. Where the rules read a statement and the model disagrees, block for smoking, age and sex; for labs and conditions, show a note. (4) The rules read the resulting 'read as' text. That text and its ParsedPatient go into gr.State; Build uses them without calling the model and refuses if the textbox changed. (5) Failure means no substitutions plus a header line giving the reason. (6) The API defaults to reader='rules', and reader='model' also returns `read_as_text`. The builder, the corpus and the battery stay unchanged, and every value that reaches MeTTa was read by the rules from text the person can see.
